nv_bass_wall.blurb: A compact sport wall inside Arrow Canyon, northeast of Las Vegas, facing the Dirty Wall from the opposite side of the canyon floor. Roughly ten bolted lines cover the 5.10 to 5.12 range, weighted toward the harder end: five of them sit in the 5.12s, and three more in the 5.11s. Expect a steep, slick start on polished rock, then easier-angled, slightly overhanging climbing on textured stone with jugs, blocky holds and crimps. Most routes put the first or second bolt low, so a stick clip is handy. The wall is a very short walk from where you enter the canyon, which makes it an easy add-on to a day on the neighbouring walls.

nv_5_west_face.blurb: One of the walls at Owl Rock, a small high-desert sport crag outside Reno. About ten bolted lines range from 5.6 up to 5.12-, with a few in the 5.7s, three in the 5.10s and a single route each in the 5.9, 5.11 and 5.12 range, so beginners and intermediates both have something. The wall looks toward Mt Rose and catches late-afternoon light in winter. The ground at the base is sloped and uneven, so it is the one wall at Owl Rock that is a poor choice for small children. Reach it by taking the main trail toward the North Wall, then turning right and scrambling up a short zig-zag path below the left-hand arete.

nv_main_rock.blurb: The main wall of Trippy Rock, a small crag above the Nevada shore of Lake Tahoe near Incline Village. Around ten lines mix bolted sport routes with a handful of top-rope lines and one trad route. Grades run from a pair of easy 5.5 climbs through the 5.9 and 5.10 range to several 5.11s, which are the crag's main draw for steeper, harder work. The wall is seen up the hill through the trees from the climbers' path, and the anchors on top can be reached by a third-class scramble up the back, which makes setting up top-ropes straightforward. Views of the lake open up from the top.
